group.passage:
At 7:00 p.m. on August 23, 1989, roughly two million people from Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania stood hand in hand, forming a human chain spanning 675 kilometers. [[1]] The campaign is called the Baltic Way.
The protest was launched with a view to arresting the world’s attention to the existence of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, a treaty inked by the foreign ministers of the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany half a century before. [[2]] The daring move led to the outbreak of the Second World War as well as the Soviet invasion of the Baltic countries.
The event was orchestrated by the popular front parties in the Baltic countries. The organizers mapped out ideal locations from towns to cities so that the chain would not be broken. No one knew whether the political campaign would be successful, since there were no mobile phones at that time. [[3]] People who would like to participate in the event should stay tuned, listening to impassioned speeches delivered by the leading activists.
In retrospect, Anne-Marie Riitsaar said she had mixed feelings on that day. She and her parents took part in the Baltic Way. When they made it to the highway, it was crowded with people holding hands. Everyone was smiling, singing, and hugging each other. Their joy permeated the air. However, fear and confusion could also be felt on that occasion, since no one was sure whether the protest would end up in success.
[[4]] It showcased solidarity among the three countries. After the social movement, the very day became an official remembrance day known as the Black Ribbon Day.

options_bank.A: The announcement of the exact timing was made through radio broadcasts.
options_bank.B: It was a peaceful political demonstration against the illegal Soviet occupation.
options_bank.C: As it turned out, the non-violent protest, thanks to all the participants’ undying enthusiasm for independence, was an important milestone in history.
options_bank.D: According to the secret protocols in the pact, the two powers divided Poland, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Romania into their respective spheres of influence.
